subChunks.title: React 19 — New Features and Patterns
subChunks.hookHtml: React 19 is the most significant update since hooks. The use() hook reads promises and context in render. Actions replace the useFormStatus/useFormState pattern with a unified model. The compiler (formerly React Forget) eliminates most manual memoisation. ref is now a prop. Context.Provider is gone. These changes simplify patterns that required ceremony in React 18 — understanding them lets you write less code that does more.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The `use()` hook

import { use, Suspense } from 'react';

// use() reads a promise — suspends until resolved:
function QuestDetails({ questPromise }: { questPromise: Promise<Quest> }) {
  const quest = use(questPromise); // Suspends if pending, throws if rejected
  return <div>{quest.title}</div>;
}

// Wrap in Suspense + ErrorBoundary:
<ErrorBoundary fallback={<ErrorPage />}>
  <Suspense fallback={<QuestSkeleton />}>
    <QuestDetails questPromise={fetchQuest(id)} />
  </Suspense>
</ErrorBoundary>

// use() also reads context — but conditionally (unlike useContext!):
function ThemedButton({ variant }: { variant: 'primary' | 'ghost' }) {
  // Can be called inside if/for/try — unlike hooks:
  if (variant === 'primary') {
    const theme = use(ThemeContext);
    return <button style={{ color: theme.primary }}>...</button>;
  }
  return <button>...</button>;
}

Actions and useActionState

// React 19 replaces useFormState + useFormStatus with useActionState:
import { useActionState } from 'react';

async function acceptQuestAction(prevState: State, formData: FormData) {
  const questId = formData.get('questId') as string;
  try {
    await acceptQuest(questId);
    return { success: true, error: null };
  } catch (e) {
    return { success: false, error: e.message };
  }
}

function AcceptQuestForm({ questId }: { questId: string }) {
  const [state, dispatch, isPending] = useActionState(acceptQuestAction, {
    success: false,
    error: null,
  });

  return (
    <form action={dispatch}>
      <input type="hidden" name="questId" value={questId} />
      {state.error && <p role="alert">{state.error}</p>}
      {state.success && <p>Quest accepted!</p>}
      <button type="submit" disabled={isPending}>
        {isPending ? 'Accepting...' : 'Accept Quest'}
      </button>
    </form>
  );
}

useOptimistic

import { useOptimistic, useActionState } from 'react';

function QuestList({ quests }: { quests: Quest[] }) {
  const [optimisticQuests, addOptimisticQuest] = useOptimistic(
    quests,
    (state, acceptedId: string) =>
      state.map(q => q.id === acceptedId ? { ...q, status: 'ACCEPTED' } : q)
  );

  async function handleAccept(questId: string) {
    addOptimisticQuest(questId);  // UI updates immediately
    await acceptQuest(questId);   // Server mutation
    // On error, React reverts to the last stable value automatically
  }

  return (
    <ul>
      {optimisticQuests.map(quest => (
        <li key={quest.id}>
          {quest.title} — {quest.status}
          <button onClick={() => handleAccept(quest.id)}>Accept</button>
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

ref as a prop + cleanup

// React 19: ref is a regular prop — no forwardRef needed:
function Input({ ref, ...props }: React.InputHTMLAttributes<HTMLInputElement> & {
  ref?: React.Ref<HTMLInputElement>
}) {
  return <input ref={ref} {...props} />;
}

// Parent:
const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);
<Input ref={inputRef} placeholder="Quest title" />

// Ref cleanup (new in React 19):
function FocusTrap({ children }) {
  return (
    <div
      ref={(node) => {
        if (node) {
          node.focus();
          // Return cleanup function:
          return () => node.blur();
        }
      }}
    >
      {children}
    </div>
  );
}

Context without Provider

// React 19: use ThemeContext directly instead of ThemeContext.Provider:
const ThemeContext = createContext('light');

// Before (React 18):
<ThemeContext.Provider value="dark">
  {children}
</ThemeContext.Provider>

// React 19:
<ThemeContext value="dark">
  {children}
</ThemeContext>

Vex: "React 19's compiler is the most impactful change for existing codebases — it automatically applies memoisation that you would have written with useMemo and useCallback. But don't wait for the compiler to fix performance problems; understand why they exist first. The compiler optimises correct code; it doesn't fix incorrect code."

storyBeats.text: React 19. The compiler ships. Two hundred useMemo calls made redundant overnight. The forms all use useActionState — no more useFormStatus in a separate component. The use() hook reads promises without useEffect. The ceremony is gone.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: React 19 removes boilerplate that existed to work around limitations. forwardRef existed because ref wasn't a prop. useFormStatus existed because form state was local. useOptimistic codifies a pattern everyone was implementing manually. Learn these patterns — they'll be the standard for the next several years.

storyBeats.speaker: useActionState replaces useFormState + useFormStatus

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Migrate React 18 patterns to React 19:

  • Replace a useFormState + useFormStatus form with useActionState that manages loading state, error state, and success state in one hook
  • Replace a manual optimistic update (useState + server call + rollback) with useOptimistic
  • Replace a forwardRef component with a React 19 ref-as-prop component
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Upgrade the quest board to React 19 patterns: (1) Replace all useFormState + useFormStatus pairs with useActionState — verify the isPending state correctly disables submit buttons. (2) Replace manual optimistic update logic in the quest acceptance flow with useOptimistic — test that UI updates immediately and reverts on error. (3) Remove all forwardRef wrappers from your Input, Select, and Textarea components and pass ref as a regular prop. (4) Update Context providers from <ThemeContext.Provider value="..."> to <ThemeContext value="...">. Document the lines of code removed from each change.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what `use()` does and why it's different from `useContext` and `useState` — specifically, what does it mean that `use()` can be called conditionally? Walk through `useOptimistic` — what happens to the optimistic value if the server mutation fails? Explain why the React 19 compiler eliminates most useMemo/useCallback — what does it analyse, and why doesn't it require you to change your code?

questions.prompt: A component uses `const quest = use(questPromise)`. The promise rejects. What happens?
options: The rejection propagates as a thrown error — the nearest ErrorBoundary catches it and renders its fallback. Without an ErrorBoundary, the error propagates to the root.
use() returns undefined when the promise rejects
React re-renders the component with quest set to null
use() catches the rejection automatically and returns a default value
questions.answer: The rejection propagates as a thrown error — the nearest ErrorBoundary catches it and renders its fallback. Without an ErrorBoundary, the error propagates to the root.
questions.explanation: use() is designed to work with the Suspense + ErrorBoundary model: pending → Suspense fallback, resolved → component renders, rejected → ErrorBoundary catches. This is why components using use() should always be wrapped in both an ErrorBoundary (for rejections) and a Suspense (for pending). The pattern is consistent: you never need to check 'did the promise fail?' in component code — that's the error boundary's job.

questions.prompt: When should you still manually add `useMemo` even with the React 19 compiler?
options: When the expensive computation's result is passed to a non-React consumer (a Canvas API, a WebWorker, a third-party library) that can't be tracked by the compiler — the compiler only optimises React re-renders, not external computations
Never — the compiler handles all optimisation automatically
When the computation takes more than 100ms
When the component has more than 10 props
questions.answer: When the expensive computation's result is passed to a non-React consumer (a Canvas API, a WebWorker, a third-party library) that can't be tracked by the compiler — the compiler only optimises React re-renders, not external computations
questions.explanation: The React 19 compiler optimises memoisation for React's reconciliation — it knows when props/state change and when re-renders are unnecessary. It doesn't know about external effects: if you compute a complex data structure and pass it to a Canvas drawing function, the compiler can't track whether the Canvas needs to redraw. In these cases, useMemo with explicit deps is still the right tool. The compiler also won't add memoisation inside dynamic patterns it can't statically analyse.
